I’ve got the debugging workflow loaded. First pass now is evidence gathering: repo shape, simulator entry points, and whatever trace/profiling hooks already exist, so any candidate I return is tied to measured scheduler behavior rather than guesswork.

The worktree is already dirty (`perf_takehome.py`, benchmark/log docs, plus `skills/`), so I’m treating all existing changes as user state and won’t touch them. Next I’m reading the simulator and tests to understand exactly what “official cycles” means here.

The history files line up with your stated 1053 best: the current candidate has 2043 load slots and a 1053-cycle schedule, so the theoretical load floor is `ceil(2043/2)=1022`. That means the entire problem I’m tracing is only 31 cycles above the raw load-slot lower bound, which is usefully tight.
Small environment note: `python` isn’t on PATH here, so I’m switching the same verification to `python3` with bytecode writing disabled.
`python3` is too old for the simulator’s `match` syntax, so I’m checking the local Python options before doing any profiling. No code changes, just finding the right interpreter.
There’s a Homebrew Python 3.14 available; I’ll use `/opt/homebrew/bin/python3.14` for all simulator runs.

Baseline verification passed with 1053 cycles on the official test script. Now I’m profiling the built `kb.instrs` directly instead of regenerating `trace.json`, so the repo stays untouched while we still get cycle-by-cycle load-slot evidence.

The idle-load picture is now pretty sharp: 1021 of 1053 cycles have both load slots full; the 63 idle load slots are concentrated before the first real gather and after the last one, with only one anti-dep-related half-idle cycle at cycle 35. Scheduler-only probing so far: all 120 engine-order permutations tie or lose at 1053+, and simple tie-break changes lose or tie. Notably, moving `load` later fills the anti-dep half-hole differently but still lands at 1053, so the remaining gap is not a simple engine-order artifact.

I also checked the code path for `stagger`: in this snapshot it is assigned once and never read, so changing it alone cannot affect the schedule. The knobs that actually change task emission are `group_offsets`, `n_groups`, selected block sets, and scheduler policy.

The offset sweep is still running; it is building schedules in memory only. While it runs, the key measurement to keep in view is that the current schedule has just two load-offset bursts: a 4-cycle warm-up burst for block 0, then a nearly solid 979-cycle load-offset stream from cycle 64 to 1042.

This sweep is a little chunky because it recompiles the unrolled kernel for each variant, but it’s bounded: single-coordinate plus adjacent-pair offset perturbations. I’m letting it finish because even “no improvement” is useful evidence here.

The offset perturbation sweep confirms the current neighborhood: no single-offset or adjacent-pair change improved 1053. A few ties exist (`group_offsets[2]=5` and `group_offsets[5]=9`), but they preserve the same load histogram rather than creating new slack.

I’m adding one more scheduler probe focused on “tasks that unlock future loads” rather than generic longest-path priority. If this loses, it will strengthen the conclusion that the remaining 31-cycle gap is mostly dependency-shape, not scheduler sorting.

The load-descendant priority variants also tie or lose. Prioritizing future load unlocks too aggressively actually delays the first `load_offset` from cycle 59 to 60 or even 80, so the current longest-path priority is already doing the right thing for this DAG.

The only anti-dep-related load hole I found is cycle 35, where `scratch_scalar`/`scratch_addr` reuse blocks a tree preload. Treating anti-deps more conservatively is expected to hurt; the more interesting question was whether making them more same-cycle friendly helps, and the engine-order sweep suggests it only reshuffles holes, not total cycles.

A weird inconsistency popped up: a direct import now reports a 1052-cycle instruction stream, while the official test run earlier printed 1053. I’m going to pin this down before making any claims; it may be stale bytecode, an import-path difference, or a dirty-worktree source mismatch.

The inconsistency is real: the current `perf_takehome.py` on disk now verifies at 1052 official cycles, and its contents differ from the earlier snapshot I first read. I’m treating that as external/user state and continuing read-only from the current on-disk file; I’ll call out the 1052 vs. the 1053 assumption in the final.

I’m rerunning the scheduler sweeps on the current 1052-cycle snapshot now. The shape is similar but the instruction mix changed slightly: 2040 loads, 880 flow, 6008 VALU, and the load floor is now 1020 cycles.

On the current snapshot, scheduler results are still flat: many engine orders tie at 1052, but none beat it. `pos_i` can pull the first `load_offset` to cycle 57, yet the tail remains at 1041 and total cycles stay unchanged.

Offset and `n_groups` sweeps are running again against the 1052 snapshot. I’ve narrowed this one to single-offset perturbations and derived regroupings, since the earlier adjacent-pair sweep already matched your “no better nearby” note.

The current offset/regrouping sweep produced ties but no improvement. Interesting ties: `n_groups=10` with offsets `[0,6,8,8,12,17,15,19,20,22]`, `n_groups=16` derived offsets, and `n_groups=20` derived offsets all still schedule at 1052, so the grouping surface has multiple plateaus but no obvious lower point from these knobs.

One final read-only probe: I’m swapping which blocks get the fixed-size final/early depth-4 precompute, preserving total load count. That tests whether the load-offset burst placement can be improved without “winning” by deleting more loads.

The block-swap sweep is still running. If it finds only ties/losses, the actionable conclusion will be that further improvement likely needs changing the DAG itself, not just moving the existing load-offset burst around.

Good find: preserving the same total load count, swapping block `2` into `final_depth4_select_blocks` in place of one of `{3,5,9,10}` builds a 1051-cycle schedule in scratch. I’m validating one of those in memory now for correctness against the frozen simulator shape before I report it as a candidate.

The 1051 scratch candidate validated on 10 frozen-simulator seeds. I’ll do a small combination check now: the same block swap plus offset/scheduler variants, to see whether it is a plateau at 1051 or can be nudged once more.
The combination sweep is in progress. It’s checking whether the validated 1051 block-swap candidate has an offset or engine-order pairing that drops another cycle.

The 1051 candidate appears to be a plateau too: small offset changes and engine-order changes tie but do not beat it. The useful concrete candidate is the final-depth4 block swap, not a scheduler-policy rewrite.

For the validated 1051 variant, the two load-offset bursts merge into one continuous cycle range `58-1040`; that is exactly the missing cycle it saves versus current `58-61` plus `63-1041`. Nice, this is a real burst-placement win with unchanged load count.

All four 1051 block-swap variants validated on a few frozen-simulator seeds. I’m doing the final verification pass now: official current cycles, tests diff, and a clean summary of what is measured versus just a candidate.
Using `superpowers:verification-before-completion` for the close-out evidence. I’ll run the official test command fresh and check the tests diff before I summarize.
